title: NGC 3359 – Meet Me at the Bar
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 3359, imaged by the Gemini North telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A round pinwheel of spiral arms surrounds a straight bar running through the centre of NGC 3359. Light red patches dotted across the disk mark places where new stars are forming. The galaxy lies in Ursa Major and was imaged with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North, on Mauna Kea in Hawai‘i.

The spiral arms make NGC 3359 easy to classify as a spiral galaxy, but its central bar sets it apart from many others. Research suggests the bar is young, only about 500 million years old, while the galaxy itself is several billion years old. Astronomers are still working out how such large bars form and how long they last.

The red patches are H II regions: clouds of hydrogen lit up by young stars recently born inside them. NGC 3359 holds roughly 100 of them, a sign of intense star formation. The Orion Nebula is a familiar example of this kind of region in our own galaxy.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North; the g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha images are shown as blue, green, orange and red.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter picks out the red glow of hydrogen, making star-forming regions stand out more strongly than they would to the eye.

explore: The caption describes NGC 3359 as a relatively close spiral, at a distance of roughly 49 million light-years. Its apparent magnitude is 10.5, so it is easily visible in portable amateur telescopes. This image covers 4.3 by 5.3 arcminutes of sky.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a straight central bar and pinwheel arms dotted with light red patches.
